temptingClaims: Length contraction is what a camera would see: a moving sphere would look flattened in a photograph.
whyTempting: § 4 says that a moving sphere, viewed from the stationary system, has the shape of an ellipsoid, and that its length along the motion appears shortened. “Viewed” and “appears” sound like seen, and a photograph is the everyday meaning of how something looks.
whereItIsTrue: The shape § 4 finds is real in its own sense: it is where the surface is at one time of the stationary system, measured with that system's rods and synchronized clocks, an ellipsoid shortened along the motion in the ratio \(1 : \sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\) (p. 903).

whatIsTrue.r0: § 4's ellipsoid is the set of positions the surface occupies at one instant of the stationary system. A camera records light that arrives together, which left different parts of the body at different times. That is a different question, and the paper does not treat it.
whatIsTrue.r1: The paper takes a rigid sphere of radius \(R\) at rest in the moving system k and writes its surface in the coordinates \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) of the stationary system K at the time \(t=0\): \(\frac{x^2}{\left(\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{V}\right)^2}\right)^2}+y^2+z^2=R^2\), an ellipsoid of revolution with the axes \(R\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\), \(R\), \(R\) (p. 903). “At the time \(t=0\)” is the point: the shape is built from positions taken simultaneously in K, by the clocks § 1 synchronizes. A photograph gathers the light that reaches the lens at one moment; light from the far side of a moving body left it earlier than light from the near side, so a picture combines positions from different times, and what it shows needs its own calculation. SR-03's moving-sphere preset gives the paper's ellipsoid, axes 0.8, 1 and 1 for \(R=1\) at \(v=0.6\,V\), and its manifest lists optical camera appearance among what it does not model.
whatIsTrue.r2: (1) The sphere at rest in k: every point of its surface lies at the distance \(R\) from its centre. (2) Carry the surface into K with the equations of § 3 and fix one time of K, \(t=0\): it becomes \(\frac{x^2}{1-(v/V)^2}+y^2+z^2=R^2\) (p. 903). (3) Read off the axes: along the motion \(R\sqrt{1-(v/V)^2}\), across it \(R\). (4) At \(v=0.6\,V\): \(\sqrt{1-0.36}=0.8\), so the axes are \(0.8\,R\), \(R\), \(R\). (5) Each point of that surface is a position at the same time of K, found with rods and synchronized clocks. A camera collects light arriving at one moment, which left nearer and farther parts of the body at different times, so a photograph answers a different question from the one § 4 answers.
whatIsTrue.r3: What a camera or an eye would record of a fast-moving body was taken up in 1959 in J. Terrell's 'Invisibility of the Lorentz Contraction' and R. Penrose's 'The apparent shape of a relativistically moving sphere', whose titles state their subject. The paper does not treat the question, and this record has not read those papers and gives no account of their results.

sources: A. Einstein, Ann. Phys. (4) 17, 891–921 (1905), plate p. 903
